"I will not permit it!" he exclaimed, his face a thundercloud of fury. "You shall not throw your life away on this... this fortune hunter!"

"She is nothing of the sort!" I cried, my own temper rising to meet his. "You do not know her; you have no right to speak of her so!"

"I have every right! I am your guardian, Julian, and I have stood in the place of your father for fifteen years. Am I to watch you undo all our family has built for the sake of a pretty face and a deceitful tongue?"

"Deceitful? Uncle, what can you mean by this? What is this poison you have taken against Eleanor? Is it her lack of a great name or dowry? Is our position so precarious that it cannot withstand a marriage for love?"

He turned from me, pacing the room in his agitation, his hands clasped tightly behind his back. "Love! You are a boy, you know nothing of it. You know nothing of anything!"

"Then enlighten me!" I insisted, stepping in front of him and forcing him to stop. "What is this dark mystery you hint at? Why did you turn so pale when I mentioned her family name, Verney? What do you know of them?"

He looked at me then, and I saw not anger, but a profound and weary sorrow in his eyes, a look that frightened me more than his rage. "Some things are better left buried, Julian. For your own sake, for your own happiness, give this girl up."

"Never," I said, my voice low and resolute. "Not until you give me a reason. A true reason."

He opened his mouth to speak, but at that very moment the heavy oak door to the library swung open without a knock. It was Hobbes, the butler, looking deeply unsettled.

"Your pardon, Mr. Armitage," he began, his voice strained. "But there is a person here who insists on seeing you. He would not give a name, sir."

"I am seeing no one, Hobbes. Send him away at once!" my uncle snapped, his irritation returning.

"I tried, sir, believe me. He is a... a most determined sort of gentleman, sir. He said to give you this, and that you would know what it meant."

Hobbes extended a silver tray, and upon it lay not a note, but a single, tarnished brass key of an old and unusual design. My uncle stared at it, and all the color drained from his face. For a moment, I thought he might faint. He reached out a trembling hand and took the key, his fingers closing around it as if it were a holy relic.

"Very well, Hobbes," he said, his voice a mere whisper. "Show the gentleman into the West study. And see that we are not disturbed. On any account."

He turned to me, a new, almost frantic light in his eye. "Julian, you must go now. We will speak of this tomorrow. Everything... everything will be made clear tomorrow. Trust me in this, my boy. Do not judge me harshly until you know all."

"But this key, this man," I began, bewildered. "What has this to do with Eleanor?"

"It has everything to do with her!" he cried out, his composure shattering again. "Now go! Leave me, for pity's sake!"

I bowed, my mind a whirlwind of confusion and suspicion, and left the room. What terrible drama had I unearthed? Who was this man, and what power did his simple key hold over my stern and formidable uncle? I had to see Eleanor; I had to warn her, though of what, I did not know.

I found her in the conservatory, sketching the late-blooming orchids with a focused, delicate hand. The sight of her calmed the tempest in my soul, if only for a moment.

"My dear Julian," she said, looking up with a smile that faltered as she saw my face. "What is it? You look as though you have seen a ghost."

I smiled grimly. "Perhaps I have; the ghost of some old sin, I think. I have spoken with my uncle, Eleanor. I told him of my intentions."

Her charcoal pencil stilled. She looked down at her sketch, her posture suddenly guarded. "And I can surmise his response. He was not... pleased."

"That is the mildest of terms for it. But it was more than mere snobbery, Eleanor. He became a different man. He spoke of dark secrets. And he knew your name, your family name, Verney."

She met my gaze, her lovely brown eyes wide with an unreadable expression. "Did he now? And what did Mr. Armitage have to say of the Verneys?"

"Nothing and everything. He begged me to give you up, for my own happiness. As if such a thing were possible! He says tomorrow he will explain all. But Eleanor, I feel I am walking into a trap."

She rose and came to me, placing a cool hand on my arm. Her expression was one of profound sadness. "Perhaps you should listen to him, Julian. He is a wise man; he has your best interests at heart. I am not worthy of the trouble I am causing. There are other women, better women..."

"Stop," I said, catching her hand in mine and raising it to my lips. "Do not say such things. Do you think my love is so shallow? That a word of warning from a frightened old man could sway me? No, my darling. You are my world. Whatever this secret is, we will face it together. Let tomorrow bring its revelations; it will not change the one truth I hold to. I will not give you up."

She looked at me, her eyes glistening with unshed tears. "Oh, Julian," she whispered, her voice full of a wondering despair. "You foolish, wonderful man. You have no idea what you are saying."
